newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE TAKES EARLY LEAD IN U.S. OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE TAKES EARLY LEAD IN U.S. OPEN.

text.p: Colin Montgomerie, taking advantage of his accurate driving on an extremely long course, jumped into the early first-round lead in the U.S. Open on Thursday, going four under par in the first 12 holes for a three-stroke lead.

Montgomerie, who just won the European Grand Prix last week, started out with six consecutive pars and then birdied the seventh and ninth holes to be the only player to make the turn at two under par. He then birdied the 10th and 11th holes to stand atop the leaderboard early on a warm, cloudy day.
However, most of the 156-man field had yet to tee off on Congressional Country Club's 7,213-yard, par-70 Blue Course, the longest ever used for a U.S. Open.

Most prominent among the later starters was Masters champion Tiger Woods, who was due to tee off at noon EDT (1600 GMT), along with defending champion Steve Jones and British Open champion Tom Lehman.

Among those who made the turn at one under par in the early going were four-time champion Jack Nicklaus, the oldest player in the field at age 57, Nick Price of Zimbabwe, Grant Waite of New Zealand and young American Stewart Cink.
Nicklaus, playing in his 41st consecutive Open and 150th major championship, started slowly with a bogey at the first, but he then birdied the fifth and eighth holes to make the turn at one-under 34.
However, Nicklaus double-bogeyed the 11th and bogeyed the 13th to fall off the pace. His son, Gary, 28, was playing later in the day.
Price, winner of the British Open and two PGA Championshhips, made three birdies and two bogeys in the first six holes to make the turn at one under.

Cink, a struggling young pro, made birdies on the eighth and ninth holes to more than offset a bogey at the 5th. Cink, player of the year on the satellite Nike Tour last year, also played well in his first U.S. Open a year ago, finishing joint 16th at Oakland Hills.

Briton Ian Woosnam, the 1991 Masters champion, made three consecutive birdies from the sixth through eighth holes. He then followed with three bogeys in a row and added another to make the turn at 36.
Davis Love, who finished joint second last year, also went out in one over, following a bogey on the first hole with eight pars.
Paul McGinley of Ireland had jumped out to a very early lead with three birdies in the first five holes, but he then bogeyed the next three to stand at level par.
Congressional, which has exceptionally think rough, 100 sand bunkers and four treacherous water holes, was not kind to everyone, however.
Greg Norman, the top-ranked player in the world, made four bogeys on the front nine to go out in 39, as did lefty Phil Mickelson, who made a double bogey and three bogeys along with a lone birdie.
Curtis Strange, the last player to win back-to-back Opens in 1988-1989, also struggled, making three bogeys for 38.
Among the very early starters, Ted Tryba posted the worst front-nine score, a seven-over 42.
